Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Economy Achievements of ‘New Economy’ must be measured by sustained improvements in economic growth, employment and productivity – Dr. Nsafoah Source : Joy Business 16 November 2026 4:05pm Dr. Dennis Nsafoah ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
A US-based Assistant Professor of Economics at Niagara University, Dr. Dennis Nsafoah, wants the success of the New Economy measured by sustained improvements in economic growth, employment, and productivity.
According to him, the New Economy cannot ultimately be judged by the size of its capital budget.
Before the 2027 Budget, he raised three questions: How much of the additional fiscal space would be devoted to new public investment? How would the government finance the programme? And how would it reconcile an ambitious reserve-accumulation agenda with urgent investment needs?
According to him, the budget offers satisfactory answers to all three.
In his commentary on the budget titled “Ghana's 2027 Budget: From Macroeconomic Stability to Prioritising Public Investment”, Dr. Nsafoah said the 2027 Budget identifies a markedly larger public investment envelope, communicates a mainly domestic financing strategy and offers a measured formal reserve-adequacy benchmark. “These are reasons for a constructive assessment, not a guarantee of success”.
Dr. Nsafoah, who is also a member of the Board of Tesah Capital also said the most consequential risk is the capacity to finance new investments while repeatedly refinancing the inherited stock of domestic obligations at sustainable cost. “That risk deserves monitoring, but not alarmism”, he pointed out.
“Ultimately, I will judge the New Economy by whether Ghana produces more per worker, attracts additional private investment, creates durable jobs and achieves sustained growth—not by how large the capital budget appears on presentation day. The government has made a promising allocation choice. The economic verdict must follow the results”, he explained.
Financing the New Economy: Domestic Borrowing and Its Implications
The government in the 2027 Budget clearly identified how it intends to finance the New Economy programme.
The 2027 cash deficit is budgeted at GH¢65.8 billion (3.6% of Gross Domestic Product), with GH¢85.0 billion in net domestic financing and GH¢17.7 billion in net external repayments.
In effect, Dr. Nsafoah said the domestic markets will fund both the fiscal deficit and the net repayment to foreign creditors, highlighting that the budget projects GH¢59.0 billion in net financing from commercial banks and GH¢25.9 billion from non-bank investors.
He stressed that limited new external borrowing reduces exposure to new foreign-currency debt, but places greater demands on domestic financial intermediation.
He added that the more important concern is the government's gross financing requirement and the associated refinancing risk, rather than the GH¢85 billion in net domestic borrowing alone.
“Beyond financing new expenditure, the government must also repay or refinance maturing Treasury bills and other domestic debt obligations. Ghana's substantial stock of short-term government securities, together with significant debt maturities scheduled for 2027 and 2028, creates additional pressure on domestic financial markets”, he warned.
Consequently, he said the government's ability to sustain its investment programme will depend partly on its capacity to manage these refinancing obligations while maintaining favourable borrowing conditions.
